text: The Boeing Company, along with its subsidiaries, is one of the world’s major aerospace firms and operates in four reportable segments: Commercial Airplanes (BCA), Defense, Space & Security (BDS), Global Services (BGS), and Boeing Capital (BCC). The Commercial Airplanes segment develops, produces, and markets commercial jet aircraft to the global airline industry, offering a family of jetliners including the 737 narrow-body and 767, 777, and 787 wide-body models, with production of the 747 ending in 2022. Development continues on the 777X program and the 737-7 and 737-10 derivatives. The Defense, Space & Security segment produces and modifies manned and unmanned military aircraft, weapons systems, and related products such as strategic defense systems, C4ISR, cyber solutions, satellite systems, and space exploration. The Global Services segment provides a full range of services to commercial and defense customers, including supply chain management, engineering, maintenance, upgrades, spare parts, training, technical documentation, and data analytics. Boeing Capital provides financing to customers to purchase and take delivery of Boeing products, managing financing exposure through equipment leases, sales-type/finance leases, notes, receivables, assets held for sale or re-lease, and investments. Boeing owns numerous patents and licenses intellectual property from third parties, including U.S. government licenses for inventions developed under government contracts, and also relies on unpatented research, engineering skills, trademarks, trade secrets, and other intellectual property. As of December 31, 2022, Boeing’s total workforce was approximately 156,000, with 13% located outside the U.S., and included about 50,000 union members. The company has major collective bargaining agreements with the International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers (20% of employees, expiring in September 2024 and July 2025), the Society of Professional Engineering Employees in Aerospace (10%, expiring in October 2026), and the United Automobile, Aerospace and Agricultural Implement Workers of America (1%, expiring in April 2027). Boeing is committed to diversity and inclusion, with a workforce composition in the U.S. as of December 2021 of approximately 23% women, 33% U.S. racial and ethnic minorities, and 15% U.S. veterans, and supports over 15,000 participants in 170 global Business Resource Groups. In 2022, Boeing hired approximately 23,000 new employees for critical skills, with a 78% offer acceptance rate and a voluntary resignation rate of about 4%. Employees engage in ongoing feedback through surveys from pre-hire to exit, and the company maintains a multi-level recognition program for performance. In 2022, Boeing employees completed approximately 5.8 million hours of learning, with over 9,000 employees annually using tuition assistance to pursue degrees, certificates, or courses from more than 300 accredited institutions worldwide. Safety, quality, integrity, and sustainability are central to Boeing’s operations, with a commitment to zero workplace injuries and an annual Code of Conduct signed by employees to uphold ethical and compliant work practices. Employees can report concerns related to ethics or safety through multiple channels, and the company addresses such concerns to uphold its values. The commercial jet aircraft market is highly competitive, with strong international competitors such as Airbus and emerging players from China, and Boeing focuses on product improvements, cost reduction, and delivering superior design, safety, efficiency, and value. The Defense, Space & Security segment competes with Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Raytheon Technologies, General Dynamics, SpaceX, and non-U.S. companies like BAE Systems and Airbus Group, which are expanding their U.S. presence through partnerships. In the commercial and defense services markets, BGS faces similar competition and intends to grow market share through high customer satisfaction and productivity. Boeing’s businesses are heavily regulated, working with U.S. government agencies such as the U.S. military, NASA, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), and the Department of Homeland Security, as well as equivalent authorities in non-U.S. markets. Government contracts may be terminated at the government’s convenience or for default; in the case of convenience termination, Boeing is entitled to payment for completed work and allowable termination costs, while in default termination, the government pays only for accepted work and may require Boeing to cover the cost difference to reprocure the items. For default, Boeing may also face liability for damages. Commercial aircraft must comply with FAA regulations on production, quality, airworthiness, repair procedures, and operational safety, with new models requiring FAA certification before service; similar requirements exist outside the U.S. under national aviation authorities, coordinated in Europe by the European Union Aviation Safety Agency. Boeing is subject to environmental laws and regulations regarding the discharge, treatment, storage, disposal, and remediation of hazardous substances and wastes, as well as climate change-related laws affecting greenhouse gas emissions, which could increase compliance costs, energy and raw material expenses, and investment in new technologies. Environmental compliance costs are a normal, recurring part of operations and are often allowable under U.S. government contracts. It is reasonably possible that increased environmental compliance costs could materially impact Boeing’s results of operations, financial condition, or cash flows if stricter clean-up standards or new contamination areas are imposed. For further details on environmental contingencies, see Note 13 to the Consolidated Financial Statements. Non-U.S. sales are subject to both U.S. and non-U.S. governmental regulations and procurement policies, including import-export controls and tariffs.

Boeing’s operations are subject to environmental regulations related to climate change, including laws that limit or govern greenhouse gas emissions. These regulations could increase environmental compliance expenses, raise energy and raw material costs, and require new or additional investments in design and technology. The company continuously evaluates its environmental compliance and management to ensure adherence to all applicable laws and regulations. Investigation, remediation, and ongoing operation and maintenance costs associated with environmental compliance are routine and recurring parts of its operations, and such costs are often allowable under its U.S. government contracts. It is reasonably possible that costs to maintain environmental compliance could materially affect the company’s results of operations, financial condition, or cash flows if regulators impose stricter cleanup standards, new areas of soil, air, or groundwater contamination are discovered, or the scope of required work expands. For further details on environmental contingencies, refer to Note 13 in the Consolidated Financial Statements. Non-U.S. sales are subject to both U.S. and non-U.S. governmental regulations and procurement policies, including import-export controls, tariffs, investment rules, exchange controls, anti-corruption measures, and repatriation of earnings, and are exposed to currency, political, and economic risks. Boeing is highly dependent on the availability of key raw materials, parts, and subassemblies from suppliers and subcontractors, primarily aluminum (sheet, plate, forgings, and extrusions), titanium (sheet, plate, forgings, and extrusions), and composites (including carbon and boron). Although alternative sources exist, qualification can take a year or more. In 2022, due to the Russia-Ukraine war, Boeing suspended purchasing titanium from Russia, which did not disrupt operations because it used inventory on hand and identified alternative sources. Many major components and equipment are procured or subcontracted on a sole-source basis, and the company continues to work with a small number of sole-source suppliers to ensure supply continuity. Boeing relies on a large number of U.S. and non-U.S. suppliers and subcontractors to meet performance specifications, quality standards, and delivery schedules at anticipated costs. While the company maintains an extensive qualification and performance surveillance system to manage third-party risks, supplier or subcontractor failures could negatively affect production schedules and program profitability, jeopardizing customer commitments. The company is also dependent on affordable access to energy sources like electricity. No material portion of Boeing’s business is considered seasonal. A significant portion of Boeing’s revenue comes from commercial airlines, which are subject to market volatility. Demand for commercial aircraft is driven by long-term trends in airline passenger and cargo traffic, influenced by economic growth, political stability, airline profitability, aircraft financing, trade policies, government relations, technological advances, fuel prices, terrorism, pandemics, epidemics, and environmental regulations. The airline industry is cyclical and competitive, with significant profit swings, and deterioration in the global economy or financial instability among major customers could reduce new orders, cause delays or cancellations of contracts, or lead to lower revenues, profitability, and cash flows, especially given that the commercial aircraft backlog spans several years. Boeing enters into firm fixed-price aircraft sales contracts with indexed price escalation clauses, which could result in losses if cost overruns occur or if cost increases exceed the escalation rate. Pricing is based on fixed amounts adjusted by formulas derived from labor, commodity, and other price indices, which are outside the company’s control and can fluctuate significantly, impacting revenue and operating margins. A significant portion of revenues comes from a limited number of commercial airlines, and there is no assurance that customers will exercise purchase options, fulfill commitments, or buy additional products or services. Fleet decisions, airline consolidations, or financial difficulties among major customers could reduce revenues and limit profit opportunities. Airlines are facing rising fuel and other costs, and the global economy is experiencing high inflation. Boeing’s Commercial Airplanes business depends on maintaining a healthy production system, ensuring every aircraft meets exacting specifications, achieving production targets, successfully developing and certifying new or derivative aircraft, and meeting stringent performance and reliability standards. The business is highly complex, involving extensive coordination with U.S. and non-U.S. suppliers, skilled labor, and evolving regulatory requirements. The FAA has implemented safety reforms, including the 2018 FAA Reauthorization Act and the 2020 Aircraft Certification, Safety and Accountability Act (ACSAA). Section 116 of ACSAA prohibited the FAA from issuing a type certificate to aircraft after December 27, 2022, unless the aircraft’s flight crew alerting system met certain specifications. The Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023 amended Section 116, so applications for original or amended type certifications submitted before December 27, 2020—including those for the 737-7 and 737-10—are no longer subject to the crew alerting requirements. Beginning one year after the FAA issues a type certificate for the 737-10, any new 737 MAX aircraft must include certain safety enhancements to receive an original airworthiness certification, which are included in Boeing’s 737-10 certification application and will be evaluated by the FAA. Beginning three years after the issuance of a type certificate for the 737-10, all previously delivered 737 MAX aircraft must be retrofitted with these safety enhancements, and as the holder of the type certificate, Boeing is responsible for any associated retrofit costs. The company has provisioned for these estimated costs and does not expect them to be material. Delays in certification or incorporating safety enhancements could negatively impact future revenues, cash flows, and results of operations. Comparable agencies in other countries may adopt similar regulations, and if the FAA or similar foreign agencies implement more stringent rules, Boeing may incur additional compliance costs. The introduction of new programs or derivatives, such as the 777X, 737-7, and 737-10, involves increased risks related to meeting development, testing, certification, and production schedules. Boeing has experienced production quality issues, including in the supply chain, which contributed to reduced 787 deliveries, including a suspension from May 2021 to August 2022. The company continues inspections and rework on stored 787 aircraft. Some customers have contractual rights to compensation for late deliveries or to reject individual aircraft. Delays on the 737, 777X, and 787 programs have led to, and may continue to lead to, customer rights to terminate orders, receive compensation, or substitute orders with other Boeing aircraft. Boeing must minimize production disruptions, achieve operational stability, and implement productivity improvements to meet customer demand and maintain profitability. The company has announced plans to adjust production rates on several programs. The 787 program is currently producing at low rates and is expected to gradually increase to 5 per month in 2023. 777X production is currently paused and expected to resume in 2023. The 737 program has stabilized at 31 per month due to operational and supply chain challenges, with plans to gradually increase production based on market demand and supply chain capacity. If production changes at any commercial aircraft assembly facility are delayed or cause significant disruption, or if suppliers fail to deliver components at required cost and rates, Boeing may be unable to meet delivery schedules or achieve financial performance targets. Operational challenges, such as supplier delays, internal performance failures, or regulatory approval delays, could result in out-of-sequence work, increased production costs, delayed deliveries, impacts to aircraft performance, and higher warranty or fleet support costs. Boeing and its suppliers are experiencing supply chain disruptions due to the lingering effects of COVID-19, global supply chain constraints, and labor instability, along with inflationary pressures. These factors have reduced productivity and negatively affected financial position, results of operations, and cash flows. If Boeing’s commercial aircraft fail to meet performance or reliability requirements or required sustainability standards, the company could face additional costs or lower revenues. Developing and manufacturing aircraft to meet performance, reliability, and sustainability standards is costly and technologically challenging, especially for newer programs. Any failure of a Boeing aircraft to meet these standards could disrupt operations, increase costs, and reduce revenues. Changes in U.S. government defense spending or acquisition priorities could negatively impact financial results. A substantial portion of Boeing’s revenue comes from the U.S. government, primarily from defense programs with the U.S. Department of Defense (U.S. DoD). U.S. defense spending is difficult to predict and may be affected by the national security threat environment, national security strategy, foreign policy, domestic politics, macroeconomic conditions, and legislative actions such as authorization and appropriations bills. The timeliness of FY24 and future appropriations remains a recurring risk; a lapse in funding could cause a government shutdown, impacting operations, while Continuing Resolutions would restrict program activities and delay new programs. Long-term uncertainty persists regarding overall defense spending in FY24 and beyond, with U.S. discretionary spending, including defense, likely to face continued pressure. There remains uncertainty about future acquisition priorities and program-level appropriations, including shifts in national security and defense priorities, and tensions between modernization, sustainment, and investment in new technologies. Changes in investment priorities or budget cuts, including those from the authorizations and appropriations process, could result in reductions, cancellations, or delays of existing or future contracts or programs, materially affecting financial results. Due to ongoing uncertainty about U.S. defense spending and the evolving threat environment, the U.S. DoD is expected to emphasize affordability, innovation, cybersecurity, and delivery of technical data and software in procurement, including implementing cybersecurity compliance requirements for the Defense Industrial Base, which the supply chain may not yet be fully prepared for. Boeing and its suppliers must successfully adapt to these changing priorities or face adverse impacts on revenues and market share. The company’s ability to deliver products and services that meet customer requirements depends heavily on the performance and financial stability of its subcontractors and suppliers, as well as on the availability of skilled labor, raw materials, and components. Boeing relies on other companies, including U.S. and non-U.S. suppliers and subcontractors, to provide raw materials, integrated components, sub-assemblies, and services. Many suppliers are experiencing inflation and disruptions due to the lingering effects of COVID-19, global supply chain constraints, and labor instability. If one or more suppliers or subcontractors face financial difficulties, delivery delays, or performance issues, Boeing may be unable to meet customer commitments, negatively impacting its financial position, results of operations, and cash flows. If key raw materials such as aluminum, titanium, or composites become unavailable or are available only at very high prices, Boeing may be unable to deliver products on time or at budgeted costs. For example, in 2022, Boeing suspended purchasing titanium from Russia due to the Russia-Ukraine war. The company believes it has sufficient materials and parts to avoid near-term production disruptions, but future supply chain impacts remain possible. In some cases, Boeing depends on a single source of supply. A service disruption from such a supplier—due to geopolitical developments or performance or financial issues—could have a material adverse effect on the company’s ability to meet customer commitments or increase operating costs. Competition in the markets in which Boeing operates may reduce future contracts and sales. Competition in its markets is intense, with some competitors having more advanced engineering, manufacturing, or marketing capabilities. In the BCA business, Boeing faces aggressive international competition seeking to gain market share, while in the BDS business, defense industry consolidation, shifting government acquisition priorities, and cost pressures from U.S. and non-U.S. defense customers are intensifying competition. The BGS segment also faces competition from similar U.S. and non-U.S. companies. Increased international competition, cross-border consolidations, and U.S. procurement and compliance requirements may limit Boeing’s cost competitiveness abroad. There is no guarantee Boeing will successfully compete, and such pressures could reduce revenues and market share. A significant portion of Boeing’s revenues comes from non-U.S. sales; in 2022, non-U.S. customers—including foreign military sales (FMS)—accounted for about 41% of revenues, and this share is expected to remain substantial. Doing business internationally exposes Boeing to risks such as changes in regulatory requirements, executive orders, global trade disputes, sourcing restrictions, local funding requirements, currency fluctuations, political and economic volatility, the need for non-U.S. representatives, financing uncertainties, funding credit or guarantee limitations, taxes, export controls, tariffs, embargoes, sanctions (such as those on Russia), trade restrictions, operational complexity, compliance with local and U.S. laws, and unforeseen events like terrorism, war, epidemics, or international conflicts. Since 2018, the U.S. and China have imposed tariffs on each other’s imports, affecting certain aircraft parts Boeing procures; Boeing mitigates these costs through Duty Drawback Customs procedures. The U.S.-China trade relationship remains stalled due to economic and national security concerns. China is a key market for commercial aircraft, and Boeing has long-standing relationships with Chinese customers who are a major part of its commercial aircraft backlog. However, the resumption of 737 MAX deliveries in China is still pending final regulatory approvals, and failure to secure new orders from China could harm market share. Following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Boeing suspended operations in Russia due to sanctions and export controls, and the war has negatively impacted, and may continue to adversely impact, Boeing’s business and financial results. Deterioration in trade relations between the U.S. and other countries could materially harm Boeing’s financial position, results of operations, and cash flows. Boeing makes estimates and assumptions in accounting for contracts and programs, which involve judgment in assessing risks, estimating revenues and costs, and forecasting schedules and technical performance. Due to the size and complexity of many contracts, estimating total revenues and costs at completion is difficult and subject to many variables, including wage and benefit increases, material prices, fixed costs, and inflation indices. Incentives and penalties are considered when estimating sales and profit rates and are recorded when sufficient information is available to assess performance. Customer and supplier claims are also evaluated. For commercial aircraft programs, inventoriable production costs, tooling, and warranty costs are accumulated and charged to cost of sales by program rather than by individual units. A program is defined by an estimated number of units to be produced over a long-term effort, based on firm orders, letters of intent, and market studies. Changes in customer mix, production costs, learning curves, price escalations, derivative aircraft costs, supplier performance, negotiations, or certification issues can affect these estimates. For development programs like the 777X, 737-7, and 737-10, risks related to certification timing and conditions—such as delays or changes in certification processes—could impact program status. Any change in these estimates could adversely affect future financial performance. Because of the significant judgment involved, materially different revenues and profits could result from different assumptions, revised estimates, or changes in circumstances. Changes in assumptions or conditions could negatively affect future financial results. Boeing may not realize the anticipated benefits of mergers, acquisitions, joint ventures, or divestitures. Success depends on the ability to integrate acquired operations, the performance of the product and service portfolio, and the management team. Financial results could be harmed by unanticipated performance issues, legacy liabilities, transaction-related charges, amortization of intangible assets, asset impairments, credit guarantees, partner performance, or indemnifications. Consolidations of joint ventures could also affect reported results. While Boeing has established procedures to mitigate these risks, there is no assurance of success. Divestitures may result in continued financial involvement through guarantees or other arrangements, and nonperformance by divested businesses could lead to additional payments, higher costs, or asset write-downs. A significant portion of Boeing’s business is conducted under U.S. government contracts, which are subject to unique risks. In 2022, 40% of Boeing’s revenues came from U.S. government contracts, including FMS. These contracts are subject to extensive procurement regulations, and changes to these regulations could increase compliance costs or reduce operating margins. New regulations, climate or cyber-related disclosures, or changes to existing requirements could increase costs or lead to withheld payments or reduced future business. Proposals to raise domestic content thresholds could negatively impact Boeing’s business. U.S. government contracts may be modified, curtailed, or terminated without notice, either at the government’s convenience or for performance defaults. Funding may be reduced or withheld due to fiscal constraints, shifts in national security priorities, or through temporary funding measures like continuing resolutions. Any loss of expected funding or termination of major programs could materially harm financial results. Boeing is subject to U.S. government audits and investigations, including reviews by the Defense Contract Audit Agency and Defense Contract Management Agency, which assess cost structures, compliance with laws, and internal controls. Misclassified or inaccurately allocated costs are deemed non-reimbursable, and previously reimbursed amounts must be refunded. Inadequacies in systems or policies could result in withheld payments, penalties, or reduced future business. If an audit uncovers improper or illegal activities, Boeing could face civil or criminal penalties, contract termination, forfeiture of profits, fines, or debarment from U.S. government contracts. Reputational harm could occur even if allegations are later found false. Boeing enters into fixed-price contracts, which expose it to losses if actual costs exceed estimated revenues. In 2022, approximately 60% of BDS and 69% of BGS revenues came from fixed-price contracts. While these contracts allow for cost reductions and efficiency gains, they also carry the risk of reduced margins or losses if cost overruns occur. If estimated costs exceed estimated prices, Boeing recognizes reach-forward losses, which can significantly affect reported results. For example, in 2022, BDS recorded additional losses on several fixed-price development programs. Near-term production disruptions due to supplier issues, labor instability, and factory performance have led to significant earnings charges, expected to adversely affect future cash flows and potentially result in further charges. New programs also carry risks of reach-forward losses upon award or during performance. Estimating costs for development contracts is more uncertain than for production contracts due to complex designs and technical or quality issues that can cause delays and higher costs, leading to material charges. Key fixed-price development programs include Commercial Crew, KC-46A Tanker, MQ-25, T-7A Red Hawk, VC-25B Presidential Aircraft, and commercial and military satellites. Boeing also enters into cost-type contracts, which account for approximately 40% of BDS and 31% of BGS revenues in 2022. These often involve complex technical challenges and may have uncertain award or incentive fees earned over long periods. Financial risks include reduced fees, lower profit rates, or program cancellation due to cost, schedule, or technical performance issues. Programs such as Ground-based Midcourse Defense, Proprietary, and Space Launch System are primarily cost-type. Some contracts in the commercial satellite and government satellite industries include in-orbit incentive payments, which are paid over time or in full before final acceptance. These payments are at risk if the satellite fails to meet performance specifications for up to 15 years after acceptance. The net present value of expected in-orbit incentive fees is recognized as revenue during construction. If the satellite fails to meet performance criteria, customers may not make future payments, and Boeing may be required to refund amounts or incur significant charges. Unauthorized access to Boeing’s, its customers’, or suppliers’ information systems poses a significant risk. Boeing relies heavily on IT systems and networks, and as cyber threats grow in volume and sophistication, the risk to data confidentiality, integrity, and availability continues to evolve. A cyberattack—whether direct or through the supply chain—could result in loss of intellectual property, unauthorized access to sensitive data, operational disruption, or compromised products. Boeing maintains technical security controls, policy enforcement, monitoring systems, and a Cybersecurity Governance Council to manage these risks. In November 2022, Boeing discovered a cybersecurity incident affecting Jeppesen, a wholly owned subsidiary providing flight planning and navigation services. The incident posed no risk to flight safety and was promptly reported to law enforcement, regulators, and customers. An investigation was launched, and additional protective measures were taken. While this incident had no material impact, future incidents could have significant effects on operations and reputation. Boeing also manages information systems for customers and suppliers, many of whom face similar threats. If Boeing fails to protect their confidential, classified, or personally identifiable data, it could suffer reputational damage or financial losses. Business disruptions from threats to physical security, extreme weather, climate change, natural disasters, pandemics, or public health crises could seriously affect future sales, financial condition, or increase costs and expenses. Such disruptions could impact internal operations or those of suppliers, delaying product and service deliveries to customers. Any significant production delays or damage, manipulation, or improper use of Boeing’s or its suppliers’ data and information systems could have serious consequences.

Changes in these assumptions could significantly alter future contributions and annual costs, impacting shareholders’ equity. For U.S. government contracts, pension costs are allocated based on U.S. Cost Accounting Standards, which can affect contract profitability. We also provide health care benefits to retirees and qualifying dependents, with future costs dependent on medical cost estimates. These estimates are subject to change and affect financial statements.
